sections.history: Tirukolakka lies just beside Sirkazhi in the Kaveri delta, and is counted among the Tevaram shrines of Chola Nadu north of the river, a Paadal Petra Sthalam sung by Sambandar and Sundarar. Local tradition derives the name from Thiru, the goddess Lakshmi, who is said to have appeared here in bridal finery, a kolam, in the grove of konrai trees, the kaa. The shrine is also known as Sapthapuri, and the Lord goes by several names, Thaalapureeswarar, Sapthapureeswarar and Thalamudaiyar, the last meaning the one who holds the cymbals. Its fame rests on the childhood of Sambandar, whose birthplace and great temple are only a short distance away.
sections.architecture: This is a modest, quiet temple of the Dravidian tradition rather than a monument of great scale. The presiding Shiva is worshipped here as Thaalapureeswarar, and the goddess is honoured as Osaikodutha Nayaki, the Lady who gave the sound, also called Dhwanipradhambal. In the prakara stand shrines of Vinayaka, Somaskanda, Subramanya, Lakshmi, Shani, Bhairava and Surya. The Ananda Theertham tank lies opposite the temple, and the Surya Theertham is also reckoned before it. The sacred tree is the konrai, the golden-flowered Indian laburnum, which gives the place its old name.
sections.legends: The story of Tirukolakka belongs to the childhood of Sambandar. Having been fed the milk of wisdom at Sirkazhi, the boy set out to visit the shrines around, and at Tirukolakka he sang before the Lord, clapping his tender hands to keep the time until they grew red. Moved by the child's devotion, Shiva gave him a pair of golden cymbals, thalam. The cymbals, however, made no sound until the Goddess breathed into them the power of sound. For this the Lord is called Thalamudaiyar, the holder of the cymbals, and the Goddess Osaikodutha Nayaki, the giver of sound. Some accounts speak of golden plates rather than cymbals, but the heart of the story is the same: a child's song, and a gift that the Mother made ring.
sections.festivals: The temple's great day is bound to the festival of Sirkazhi. In Chithirai, in April and May, the Chithirai Thiruvadhirai festival is kept at the Sattainathar temple, with the milk festival on its second day. After that, the image of Sambandar is brought to Tirukolakka, where the gift of the golden cymbals is remembered. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed with devotion. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Tirukolakka is best visited as a quiet companion to Sirkazhi, a short ride away. Come to the Lord Thalamudaiyar first and then to the Goddess Osaikodutha Nayaki, pausing to remember the child who sang here with his own two hands for rhythm. The tank before the temple adds to the calm of the place. Musicians, singers and parents of young children often come to pray here, since the story speaks so tenderly of music and of a child's voice. The temple is small, and an unhurried half hour in its courtyard is enough to feel why it is loved.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again in the late afternoon and evening, with a break at midday; no firm timings could be confirmed, so check locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is usually allowed in the outer corridors and courtyard but not within the sanctums, in keeping with temple rules across Tamil Nadu. Ask the temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tirukolakka is about 2 km from Sirkazhi, close to the Ulagalandha Perumal temple, and some 19 to 20 km from both Chidambaram and Mayiladuthurai on the road between them. Sirkazhi, on the Chennai–Mayiladuthurai railway line, is the nearest station, and local buses and autorickshaws cover the short distance to the temple. Chennai is roughly 240 km away by road.
